e: What did the Romans eat? Diet from the bones

Bone collagen preserves the carbon and nitrogen isotopes of the food eaten in the last years of life. δ13C shows which plants the food chain was built on (wheat, barley, pulses: C3; millet: C4) and whether marine protein was part of it; δ15N marks the position in the food chain: the more meat, dairy or fish, the higher it is. It does not show dishes, only the source of the protein.

Source: F. De Angelis, S. Varano, A. Battistini et al., “Food at the heart of the Empire: dietary reconstruction for Imperial Rome inhabitants”, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 12 (2020) 244, doi:10.1007/s12520-020-01194-z (CC BY 4.0), Table 4; values in ‰. Of 214 bone samples 199 met the collagen quality criteria. Cemetery descriptions from the text of the paper.

For comparison the authors also measured 17 contemporary animal bones (Castel Malnome, Via Padre Semeria, the Colosseum area): δ15N is 3.8–6.7‰ for the 9 herbivores (deer, cattle, sheep, goat, hare), 4.6–6.8‰ for the 3 pigs and 9.1–10.6‰ for the 3 dogs. The human mean is 10‰ or above in all six cemeteries, i.e. similar to or higher than the dogs and well above the herbivores.

The authors’ conclusions. The diet was basically terrestrial, with C3 plants (cereals, pulses) as the plant base; consumption of C4 plants such as millet is detectable but was not widespread. There is no evidence of an exclusively marine diet; occasional fish eating cannot be ruled out, though, since up to 20% of the protein could come from the sea without showing in the collagen values. The authors explain the differences between cemeteries by what people could get in the neighbourhood where they lived. Quarto Cappello del Prete near Gabii has the lowest mean and the widest spread; most of the dead there were children.

Battistini et al., “The edge of the Empire: diet characterization of medieval Rome through stable isotope analysis”, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences 12 (2020) 196, doi:10.1007/s12520-020-01158-3 (CC BY 4.0), Tables 1 and 3; values in ‰. Of the 110 individuals sampled, Table 3 contains 101.

Six of the seven communities have means of 8.2–8.8‰, i.e. 1–3‰ lower than the imperial cemeteries (10.0–11.4‰). The authors read this as a dietary transition: with the collapse of the Empire the crisis of the trade system narrowed the range of foods available to the Romans, and less high-protein food was eaten. They see the same at Gabii (imperial 10.7‰, medieval 8.7‰). The exception is the San Pancrazio community (11.5‰), the only one where consumption of aquatic resources was detected.

Points to bear in mind. The imperial cemeteries lie outside the walls and, according to the authors, belong to the lower classes, tied to production sites or rural villas; these data say nothing about the city’s elite. δ15N can be raised by things other than diet (breastfed infants, starvation, manured fields), so a difference of a few tenths of a ‰ between cemeteries means little by itself. Some medieval samples are small (Amba Aradam 4, Piazzale Ostiense 8 individuals). A direct download from the IsoArcH database did not work; I used the published tables of the two open-access studies.
